subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: 'Primary data' is best defined as data that is:
options: Collected first-hand by the researcher for their own study
questions.explain: Primary data is collected first-hand by the researcher, e.g. via questionnaires, interviews or observation.

options: Joins the group secretly, without revealing they are a researcher
Watches from a distance using a survey
Joins the group and openly tells members they are being studied
questions.explain: In covert participant observation the researcher's identity and purpose are hidden from the group being studied.

options: Is always more reliable than primary data
Already exists, having been produced by others (e.g. official statistics, documents)
Is collected first-hand by the researcher
questions.explain: Secondary data already exists and was produced by others, such as official statistics or existing documents.

questions.q: Which is a key ethical issue researchers must consider?
options: Gaining informed consent and protecting participants from harm
Making the study as expensive as possible
questions.explain: Ethical research requires informed consent, confidentiality and protecting participants from harm.

options: Qualitative methods that explore meanings and understanding
questions.explain: Interpretivists favour qualitative methods to understand the meanings and motives behind people's actions.

options: A study can be repeated and produce consistent results
questions.explain: Reliability means a method can be repeated by others and produce consistent, similar results.

options: The results can be repeated to get the same findings
The data gives a true, authentic picture of what it claims to measure
questions.explain: Validity is about whether data is genuine and accurately reflects reality, giving a true picture.

questions.q: Positivists tend to favour methods that produce:
options: Quantitative data and seek to find patterns and causes scientifically
questions.explain: Positivists prefer quantitative, scientific methods to identify patterns and causal laws in social behaviour.

options: Contains only volunteers who feel strongly
Reflects the wider population so findings can be generalised
questions.explain: A representative sample mirrors the target population, allowing findings to be generalised to it.

questions.q: A strength of postal/self-completion questionnaires is that they:
options: Can reach large numbers of people quickly and cheaply
Always achieve a very high response rate
questions.explain: Questionnaires can gather data from many people quickly and cheaply, though response rates and depth can be limited.

questions.q: A 'structured interview' is one in which:
options: No questions are asked at all
The interviewer asks the same set of pre-decided questions in a fixed order
The conversation is free-flowing with no set questions
questions.explain: A structured interview uses a fixed set of standardised questions, making it more reliable but often less in-depth.

questions.q: Quantitative data is data in the form of:
questions.explain: Quantitative data is numerical, allowing measurement and statistical comparison.
